Angle Between Tangent And Chord

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Move a circle and a point beside it, then watch the two lines that just touch the circle. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the blue points O, R and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the chord, the inner circle and the four equal angles.

Drag O, R or C, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

A temple tablet from Ibaragi prefecture, put up in 1896, asks a surprising question: the incenter of the triangle made by two tangents sits on the circle. Drag the picture and see for yourself. The secret is the angle between a tangent and a chord.

The tangent makes a right angle

A tangent touches the circle at just one point, so the radius there is at right angles to it: OA ⟂ CA and OB ⟂ CB. Triangle OAC is right-angled, so the Pythagorean theorem gives CA² = OC² − r². The applet finds A and B by crossing the given circle with a second circle centred at C of radius √(OC² − r²). Our logic test checked that both constructions give the same points for every circle drawn.

The angle in the alternate segment

Let I′ be the midpoint of the small arc AB. The angle between tangent CA and chord AI′ cuts off the arc AI′, and the inscribed angle ∠ABI′ stands on that same arc. They are therefore equal: ∠CAI′ = ∠ABI′. The arcs AI′ and BI′ are equal, so the same argument at B gives ∠I′BC = ∠BAI′. All four marked angles match — each is ½ arccos(r / OC). The test measured all four across 3,019 circle positions, from C just outside the circle to C far away; the biggest difference was below 0.0000001.

Why the incenter lands on the circle

Those equal angles say exactly that AI′ and BI′ are the angle bisectors at A and B. Their meeting point is the incenter I, so I = I′ and the incenter lies on the given circle — the sangaku's claim. Across the same 3,019 positions the distance from O to I differed from the radius by less than 0.0000001. One small quirk is kept from the applet: its "inner circle" is drawn with radius two thirds of the true inradius, because one of the three distances it averages is measured along a line through I itself.

Tick Show hint and drag C towards the circle: the four angles grow together but never stop being equal.
